claims.text: Classical molecular dynamics with a validated multicomponent potential can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
EAM or MEAM potentials are suitable choices for FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle simulations when carefully validated.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a solid-solution structure.
A canonical-ensemble temperature ramp from room temperature to approximately 900–1200 K is appropriate for FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles between 2 and 15 nm.
Reducing FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size lowers the onset temperature for phase segregation.
Reducing FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size lowers the onset temperature for structural transformation.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio and a larger relative population of surface atoms.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles increases atomic diffusion.
Enhanced atomic diffusion drives surface segregation and phase separation in heated high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Elevated temperature can produce progressive chemical and structural evolution, including surface-layer formation, phase separation, and melting in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Thermal energy overcomes atomic bonding barriers and enables atomic rearrangement in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The larger relative share of surface atoms causes smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles to rearrange earlier than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will undergo surface segregation, phase separation, structural transformation, or melting at lower temperatures than larger particles.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles in the 2–15 nm size range under classical molecular dynamics.
Predicted segregation and transformation temperatures are sensitive to the choice and parameterization of the interatomic potential.
